name: Fillet a fish
blurb: A flexible blade following the bone structure. Round fish and flat fish need different approaches, and the yield difference between a beginner and a competent cook is enormous.
gear: A whole round fish — a trout or sea bass is a good start
steps: Scale and gut the fish if it has not been done, working in a sink to contain the mess.
Cut behind the pectoral fin down to the backbone, then turn the knife flat.
Run the blade along the backbone from head to tail in long strokes, keeping the blade angled slightly down against the bone rather than sawing.
Free the fillet over the rib cage, then remove the rib bones with a shallow cut or with tweezers.
Repeat on the other side, then skin the fillets by holding the tail and running the knife between skin and flesh at a shallow angle.
Check for pin bones by running a finger down the fillet and pull them with tweezers, in the direction they lie.
tips: Long strokes, not sawing. Sawing tears the flesh and leaves meat on the frame.
The frame tells you how you did: any meat left on the bones is yield you lost.
A sharp flexible knife matters here more than in almost any other kitchen task.
proof: Two clean, intact fillets with no pin bones and almost nothing left on the frame.
